title: The ranks
hook: by those ranged in ranks, the angels, and the believers in rows for prayer (37:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Ya-Sin with kun, and your line was be, and it is. Did you take the first step on that delayed task? Today, a new surah. Day five hundred fifty-two.

Watch the start of a Friday prayer in a big mosque, from the balcony if you can. Hundreds of people are milling around, finding spots, greeting friends. Then the call to stand comes, and something happens that looks almost choreographed. People step forward, shoulder to shoulder, heel to heel. Gaps close. Lines straighten. In a few seconds, a crowd becomes rows, as straight as if someone had drawn them with a ruler. Surah thirty-seven opens with an oath on exactly that kind of line, though the first ones it means aren't on earth.

The surah is called As-Saffat. Its first verse is an oath: wa's-saffati saffa, by those ranged in ranks. The root, s-f-f, means a row, a line. Most commentators say these are angels, standing in rows before their Lord, waiting for His command. Near the end of the same surah, in verses most commentators read as the angels speaking, they describe themselves that way: we are those who stand in ranks, and we are those who glorify. So the first rows aren't human at all. Then the hadith brings the picture down to earth. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ asks his companions: won't you line up the way the angels line up before their Lord? They ask how the angels line up. He says: they complete the front rows first, and they stand close together. Another hadith, in both Bukhari and Muslim, says: straighten your rows, for straightening the rows is part of completing the prayer. So the row isn't only tidiness. Many Muslims understand it as copying the angels. And it does something. In a row, the rich man and the driver stand shoulder to shoulder. Nobody has a reserved seat. Whoever arrives first fills the front. The line itself teaches something about equality before Allah, without anyone having to say it. As-Saffat starts with angels in ranks, and a few minutes into any congregational prayer, Muslims on earth are copying them.

The practice: straighten a row or a line. Start with yourself. Sit or stand tall, feet even, shoulders level, as if you were in a row with someone on either side. Then, if something near you is crooked, books on a shelf, shoes by the door, cups on a counter, straighten one line of them. Slowly, with care. Then return to stillness and picture the rows: angels before their Lord, and people shoulder to shoulder below. The bell holds the time.
The ranks. As-Saffat, the rows: angels standing before their Lord, and believers who straighten their lines for prayer to stand the way the angels stand. Today's word.

Your line: in ranks. Today, the next time you're in a line, at a store, a bus stop, a door, notice who's next to you, and let the line be a place where nobody's more important. Day five hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Before congregational prayer, the imam often tells the people to straighten their rows; worshippers stand shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot, filling the front rows first.

original.note: Arabic: by those ranged in ranks, the oath that opens surah thirty-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: rows are about keeping a crowd tidy.
what it means: the prayer rows copy the angels, who stand in ranks before their Lord.
what a scholar hears: 37:1 swears by as-saffat, and 37:165–166 has the angels say they stand in ranks and glorify; Muslim 430 links the human rows to theirs.
